It was an emotional speech. I can't recall precisely what he said. He was saying something about us taking a swim in the Rama lake, saying we should liberate Prozor. We had to be brave and resolute in order to reach our objective, and that then perhaps others eventually would help us, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to go back to that speech that he made for a minute. He -- so -- the first thing he mentioned was that it was going to be an inhabited area. Is that correct? This military operation was going to take place in an inhabited area.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention anything about any -- how the civilians were to be treated in this area of combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I don't recall those details. I'm not sure what was said about civilians, but I do know that in those days and in those conditions, very few people took civilians into account at all. Even if he had said something, I don't think it would have amounted to anything in practice. You have to bear in mind the situation in Prozor municipality, and this is something I spoke about in the first part of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why -- why were they not giving a thought to the civilians? Could you please very briefly tell us what was it about the culture that nobody cared about civilians?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The first part of the question was a legitimate part, and perhaps my friend should restrict herself to that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I find myself agreeing with Mr. Morrissey on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on that, please. Can you tell us why nobody was giving a thought to civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: It's difficult to say whether a thought was spared for the civilians or not. It's just that there was mounting frustration among us at the time. On the 28th of August, we had received 2.800 Bosniak refugees. They came flooding into our area. And that was in a single day. It's a ballpark figure that I'm giving you, but it could not have been less than two and a half thousand. We had also heard about what had been going on with the Bosniak civilians elsewhere. There are so many who are still listed as missing. Even as we speak, I think there's still 54 or 56 of those. It's difficult for me to recall the exact figure. That was the sort of atmosphere that prevailed. First and foremost one had to take into account the fact that the Bosniak population was facing extinction in September 1993 in Prozor municipality. As for what we could actually see from our actually positions, Uzdol was half deserted. There were far more soldiers around than civilians, but we were aware of the fact that there were still some civilians left and this was later confirmed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when General Halilovic said about the different methods to be used in this combat, what was your understanding of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I took that to mean that we were supposed to be extra careful and to look after ourselves. We were being exhorted to think back to our military training and think about what it meant to fight in an inhabited area. Potentially each house could be a point of resistance. The task itself is a lot more complex than any task we had been given up to that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the Prozor Independent Battalion - and you have touched upon this in your testimony this morning - accustomed to fighting in inhabited areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you given any guidance as to what rules have to be followed when you are engaging in an area of a theatre of war which has civilians intermingled with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to have to object at this point. I haven't objected until now because some of this evidence is relevant as to general context. But the fact of the matter is that of the ways Mr. Halilovic is charged, the duty to prevent the crime at Uzdol is not part of the indictment. I haven't sought to deal with it, I haven't cross-examined people upon it, and I'm not planning to because it's not here. So that although my friend -- I didn't objected up until this point because it's part of the narrative, frankly, this question now goes directly to one thing only, and that's failure to prevent Uzdol. And in that respect it's just an irrelevant question to the indictment that is before this Court and this Tribunal, and I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this moment I don't have the indictment at my hands. Maybe Ms. Chana could brief me on this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this point was addressed at some length in my opening speech in respect of why evidence of failure to prevent, although it is not charged in the indictment against General Halilovic, he is only charged with failure to punish in respect of Uzdol, it nevertheless, Your Honour, goes to the heart of the matter of his knowledge of the propensity of violence and thereafter to -- failure to punish. It goes to the very mens rea of his failure to punish, Your Honour. So it's extremely relevant, and I -- this objection of learned counsel is not well-founded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, when you look to the question that was asked, it's got nothing to do with the -- it's going to slip off the screen because I'm talking. When you look at the actual terms of the question that was asked, it had nothing to do with any alleged criminal tendencies of the Independent Prozor Battalion, it had to do with the question of whether Halilovic offered guidance. My learned friend may ask, of course, anything she wishes to about the battalion and about what Sefer Halilovic knew about it. I don't object to any of those questions. But this particular question was directly focused upon that issue, upon what Halilovic did, and that can only be relevant to the part of the indictment that's gone. So with respect to that, I maintain the objection and say that it is well-founded, although I hear what my friend says in response. That may be a justification for some questions, but not this one. And that's my response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this piece of the evidence is related to the charges of the failure to punish the offenders. And this is a kind of sequence of the actions which will show the case of the Prosecution. So at this stage, these questions are allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed. But I believe that you have to bear the objections from the Defence in mind that the failure for prevention is not charged in the indictment in the case of Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I stand guided by the Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us -- I've actually forgotten my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What guidance were they offered in terms of dealing with combat-inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I'm most obliged to learned counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What guidance, if any, was issued to the soldiers about how to treat the civilians in an inhabited area where -- as I said, they were at the theatre of war and the combat activities were to take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I said what General Halilovic had told us when he had us lined up outside the command, when we were assembled there rather. There were no clear and precise instructions given, nor was there any time for that, at least not the way I saw it. After that our own commander, Enver Buza, gave a speech, giving no instructions on how civilians were to be treated, or at least none that I recall. As I've said already, we had no experience to speak of in treating the civilian population during combat operations. However, we had Croatian civilians in our own territory and our experience with them was different. Those were just ordinary people living there, and I think I could go as far as to say that even the command of the Prozor Battalion did their best to serve those people, to help them, to offer assistance. As for civilians in the middle of combat operations, if you have this type of combat operation no man alive can predict what exactly will happen with the civilians. That's by way of commenting on your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. To your knowledge do you know that Sefer Halilovic was aware that the Prozor Independent Battalion had some elements within it which were part of this earlier -- what you mentioned about the abuse and the detainees? Was Sefer Halilovic aware?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I believe General Halilovic was aware of the general situation that prevailed in Prozor. We had sent a letter to him detailing the situation. In view of Prozor's importance and the importance of the broader area, in terms of how it bore on the general outcome of the war and in terms of our strategic views concerning the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina and their relations, the HVO-controlled enclave in Central Bosnia had to be linked up with Kresevo and Kiseljak. The link ran through our territory. The way the HVO treated our Bosniak civilians and any able-bodied men was a matter of general knowledge across Bosnia and Herzegovina. There were very few people who didn't know about that, particularly in view of the fact that we had issued a large number of public announcements. We regularly informed the military leadership and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We kept them informed about what was going on in the Prozor area. We were disappointed by the government's failure to deal with it. It had already been six months and the Prozor issue was never even raised. No one asked the question: What's going on there and why? That is why 1993 we felt rather isolated in our struggle to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina in that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said you wrote a letter to General Halilovic. And can you remember what date that letter was, where you drew his attention to these matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in April or possibly May 1993. We addressed our letter to him in his capacity as Chief of Staff of the supreme command. Our Territorial Defence staff and I were the ones who signed the letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, moving on from there, can you tell me when you went into battle -- and I'm going to show you a picture to assist you so you may explain to Their Honours as to how the battle unfolded. I don't know whether I've used this one already. Perhaps Ram will tell me. 0299-2292.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Have I already used this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Prosecution Exhibit P335.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll show you P335, and the other one which I would like you to -- which I'm going to show next is 2992290. Using these two. Let's look at the first one which is P335. Would you look at it. Now, if you can tell us exactly -- as you talk, you can perhaps refer to that photograph. So where did you go? And you can use this picture to describe your movements of your unit.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Our units assembled around midnight. That was between the 13th and 14th of September above the village of Here. In this photograph it might be here, at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you go along just -- when you mention a place, put a circle around it and write the name down so Their Honours can follow your testimony with some comfort.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Between the 13th and the 14th of September we assembled at night in this area above the village of Here. It's a very large stretch of territory, an open stretch of territory. You can't see it in this photograph. After having obtained logistics supplies, ammunition medical supplies, and food, our troops headed off in this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take it slowly, Witness, if you don't mind. Can you tell us where Here is, can you just mark it, as to where you assembled, in Here you said. Can you circle it again, please. This is Here --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you write "Here."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: This is Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you assemble in Here, did you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No, we didn't assemble in Here. We assembled in an area before Here, perhaps 3 or 400 metres in front of Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see it on this picture where you assembled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No, you can't see that area in this photograph. From the circle that I am now indicating, this area is perhaps 200 metres away in this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also please try and your markings within the picture. So that circle, if you can put there -- which area is that, can you just write down, please? That arrow, what are you depicting there? What's the name of this place that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: This place can't be seen in the photograph. I can't point to it in this photograph. It's an open area. There is nothing there. It's somewhat flat, but the place itself is called Lanisce, if that means anything to you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So that is the direction generally, where you've put the arrow? Let's move on. Okay. So then what happened -- where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, there's one thing I should mention. The main objective in the first stage of our action was to infiltrate the enemy ranks without being noticed, that is to say, our objective was to surprise them. But I can't say exactly where all these combat groups went. I can't tell you how they infiltrated their ranks. But I think that 80 per cent of these troops infiltrated by using this axis, if I may point to it. This is the route that they took below the village and then behind this hill. And then we reached this area. After that, the units infiltrated their ranks by taking this route in the direction of the school and other units that were supposed to secure contact with the main units that were to carry out an attack on this feature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that, the one you've just circled in the left-hand top corner? Is that Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's Uzdol. That is the primary school building. And I would also like to say that -- or rather, I would also like to tell you why this axis was selected. As I have said, this hill was under the control of the HVO. It's called Gradina. And this part is called Glavica, and the HVO positions were located there, too. In this part called Borak, the HVO also had fortified positions. I can mark these areas, HVO. And to the left of this hill there was an elevated hill controlled by the HVO. You can't see it in this photograph, but it could have a significant influence on the way in which this action is understood. These were the fortified positions that the HVO had in this limited area. In this area, we have the villages of Kranjcici and Osljani, and the artillery had been positioned there as well as one tank. And there was one tank here by the school. That is how HVO forces were deployed in this area. As far as the village Uzdol itself is concerned, I'll point to the way in which the village is spread out. In this area here you have the first houses in the village of Uzdol. They were mostly abandoned in October 1992. In this area, you can't see it very well, but there are several hamlets here. One of the hamlets is called Bobari, and then we have Pribucak, then there is Kriz, then we have Zelenike, Rajici. They're all hamlets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just put dots on these hamlets that you're talking about. Just put dots on what you've just explained, Bobari, the hamlets.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to do that in this photograph. There's not enough space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Here you have the village of Bobak [as interpreted]. You have the village of Bobari, as I have said. And here is the hamlet of Kriz. Below we have the hamlet of Rajici. And then here we have Zelenike; that's another hamlet. Then we have Budimi. There's a church here in the vicinity. All these hamlets are before the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there -- all these hamlets before you can reach the school -- the hamlets come before that military target. That's correct, is it? The HVO -- I mean, the Uzdol, which is in that big circle -- if you can put Uzdol in that big circle, please, so at least we get some sense of direction. Can you mark Uzdol, please, by writing "Uzdol" in your circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: This entire area is Uzdol. However, it's not just the school that was a military target. This was a military target, too, as well as this point here. So that couldn't have been the only military target. That would have amounted to self-destruction, in my opinion. Here you can see from the direction of Here to Uzdol there is a road. You can see it here, the one I'm pointing to here now. That is the shortest route there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Their Honours cannot see where you're pointing. They can only see when you mark. When you point at the picture, Their Honours cannot see where you are pointing. It's only when you mark it, Their Honours have a screen, and they can see all your markings. But not your pointing. So would you keep marking on the photograph and we'll just use this for demonstrative purposes. You talk about a road. If you just mark it as you talk.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That is the road, and I think that is what I said. That is the road. It's about four kilometres from Here to the school in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: But at the very beginning on this road you have the hamlet of Bobari and the fortified positions of the HVO. That's right here at this point, at the very beginning of the road. And the road passes by these positions. And there is one house here that in our opinion was also a fortified position, right by the school, or rather right by the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now I'm going to show you another photograph --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: And I'll tender this one for what its worth, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: But it does have some HVO positions in general. But I think the next photograph will be more clearer and we'll mark it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Prosecution Exhibit P337.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, I'm going to show you another photograph, and it's got more detail on it perhaps from a different direction. Now, this picture when it comes up, I would like you to explain where you yourself went. It's 0299-2290. Now, you've indicated in the last picture where HVO units and you've already marked the hills before. But this photograph, if you can just purely mark it for where your units went. And what you can do is have a broken line. If the assistant can assist him as to what the broken line is. And as he -- can you first see Krstiste hill and mark that, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah. Can you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you -- can you just write Krstiste hill, KRT?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, is that where you went, your -- your unit and draw an arrow as to how you went and where another unit went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: We didn't go there because that hill was under our control. As I have already said, our unit advanced along this axis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah, all right. So just draw a broken line, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: In my opinion, some units had already split up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where had they split up? That's what I want to know. Your unit went along this broken line. And where did the other unit go --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- from the hill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, towards the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you draw a straight line to the school, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, I can't draw the line. I didn't go there. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The direction you think the other unit went. Just even a short arrow would be good enough then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: From this point, I can only draw the line towards the school. As to whether the unit advanced along this line, I couldn't say. This is the direction, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of your unit or the other unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Of the other unit heading towards the school. I don't know exactly where the other units went. There were a number of combat groups. I can only make assumptions with regard to these other ones. All I know is the route that we followed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Anyway --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: So I will tender that also into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think there is no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The original of that photograph is Prosecution Exhibit P338, and the one that's marked is Prosecution Exhibit P339.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And is that the right time for us to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, can we please redact that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Well, you know, sometimes if the witness answers questions disclosing his identity, we'll redact it and let it go. But on the part of the Prosecution, I think I have to warn you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: I consider myself appropriately chastised, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just indicate, just so this matter goes smoothly in the future, I have written myself a little note. I have many more prior convictions than my friend has in this regard. And I think it should be the case, if it ever happens, counsel are free to warn each other and say, careful, because it can happen; I acknowledge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course. If there is no confrontation between the parties on that issue. Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Always happy to work with counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your leader you said was Osman Hero. And was he in communication with anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: He was in communication, in direct communication, with the commander Enver Buza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the technology used for this communication?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Radio communication.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So after you went off on your combat, how long did you remain in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Our units started infiltrating enemy ranks at about 2.00 in the morning. This task was completed just before daybreak. At daybreak all I can say is that all of a sudden the entire valley was on fire. It burst out into flames. And this entire period of time seemed to last no more than a second. At one point in time after my group had carried out its first task, which was to attack a fortified position that I have already indicated, that group then split up. Or it was broken up; I don't know if that's the right way to put it. But I don't know where they went after that. As I was almost unarmed, I helped withdrawing -- I helped to withdraw the wounded, and I returned to the village of Here at about 12.00. While the combat lasted, the HVO shelled the entire village. Its artillery pounded the village fiercely. And in my opinion, it was difficult to know who was firing on whom and who was fighting against whom. In the afternoon, in the early afternoon at about 12.00, about half an hour later after a partial withdrawal had been completed since the withdrawal of those units went on throughout that day, the HVO started shelling the village of Here, too. And it is in this way that the fighting on that day continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself go back to Here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before I ask -- before I carry on, I've forgotten to ask you: How many soldiers were in your unit? I mean in your combat group, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give a rough approximation so we know about some level of figures? Was it in the 10s or the 20s or the 30s or the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: There can't have been more than ten men in this group; that's for sure. But the total number of men involved in the action was over 120 because troops from a battalion from Eastern Bosnia from the Sutjeska Battalion had been attached to our groups, but I don't know how many of them exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you went back to Here, did you meet anybody in a basement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I was very tired because I had been carrying a man uphill, and I really didn't want to move from the cozy spot I had found where I could rest, but I had to because of the shells. In a newly built house, in a house that had been constructed just before the war, a house which had concrete slabs, I sought shelter and I came across Zicro Suljevic on that occasion. I don't know what his rank was, but I spoke to him on that occasion. And when the shelling started, we spoke to each other. He was very surprised by the intensity of the fire on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you have occasion to see these soldiers of the Prozor Independent Battalion after this offensive had abated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Not on that day but later, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet them, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say when I met them. Perhaps I met some of them on that day and others later on. I don't believe that I met all of them at the same time, and thus it is difficult for me to say when I met them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the casualties during this combat action from the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: We immediately found out that some ABiH members, three or four of them, had been killed. We heard something about the losses sustained by the Croatian side, but I only heard about the civilian victims through the media when listening to a local Croatian radio station a day or two afterwards. As far as the information that our soldiers provided us with is concerned, I heard nothing about that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the soldiers say about any -- any casualties, civilian or military, and the extent to you? What did you hear from them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: In the evening we immediately knew what sort of losses we had sustained, apart from the fact that we were expecting some other men to pull out, and they didn't manage to pull out so we then included them in our losses. The information we were provided with stated that we had inflicted significant losses on the HVO's manpower and apparently a tank had been destroyed, a tank that was by the school. And the artillery was either destroyed or damaged, which means that they reached the positions of the mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from the detainees any information, about the casualties, in the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: There were no detainees. But there's another thing I should mention. The Bosniaks who were in the camps in Prozor at the time, a day or two later they were engaged to clean the school. And they said that the school was spattered with blood, that there was a lot of blood and that there were traces of fighting there. I'm only referring to the school building now. In other parts of the village -- well, I didn't hear that they had been involved in cleaning up the area in the other parts of the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you heard from the Croatian media that civilians had been killed in this combative -- combat offensive, what did you do about that -- with that information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, I could provide you with some general information about the media in the war and what the task of the media in wartime is. I must inform this Tribunal of the fact that in Bosnia and Herzegovina it's generally accepted that truth is the first victim of war, and that in wartime there are very few who believe the media. And that was more or less the situation in relation to this information. We had a radio station which was the HVO's spokesperson or acted as the HVO's spokesperson. That was our attitude to -- towards the information broadcast by that radio station. And as time passed by, I believe that soon afterwards the television -- television also broadcast certain images, but it wasn't possible for us to watch television in the field at the time because we didn't have any electricity. So I didn't see those images at that time. But as time passed by, we started to suspect that civilians had been killed and that this was increasingly probable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when -- what date was it that you heard over on your own Prozor radio about civilian deaths? Can you try and recall the date, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That was perhaps a day after the withdrawal. It's really difficult to answer this question with any degree of precision. Time seemed to fly by. It was perhaps a day or two later, but I don't think as many as three.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that would possibly, by your indication, put the date from about 15th to the 16th of September, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you said, pictures were also broadcasted on the TV on that date, although you didn't see them yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I said I didn't see those images. I'm not sure if they were shown on that day or later. I don't think they could have been shown on the same day, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go and discuss this with your commander, Enver Buza?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No. By this time, the commander and I were hardly on speaking terms. Secondly, this type of behaviour - I'm not sure what I should call it - an infraction, would fall under the competence of the assistant commander for security. I didn't think it was my place to do anything about that, especially in view of the fact that by this time the commander ignored most of my explanations or reasons, even for issues that I was personally responsible for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether any report was filed against Buza in respect of these matters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I heard that General Halilovic had filed a complaint against our commander. I didn't see the complaint myself, but people were talking about it. It was also said at the time that the complaint was in relation to his actions over those days. So I can't be certain that it was about the suffering of the civilian population in Uzdol. It may in fact be the case, but I didn't see the complaint myself. This was pure hearsay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Buza, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: On the 24th of January, 1994, the Croatian army, regular troops and the HVO, launched an exceptionally fierce attack on that area. It was then that 32 of our soldiers were killed in a single day as well as a number of civilians. Fewer civilians, but there were civilian casualties. On the eve of that action, our commander had sent one-third of our troops on leave, although he had received intelligence reports previously that the Croatian side was about to launch an offensive. It was only later that I found out that the local HVO brigade, the Rama Brigade, had been involved in that operation as well as the 175th Brigade of the Croatian army stationed in Prozor at the time. They had arrived in Prozor in November or December 1993. I believe Commander Buza made a fatal error and that it was entirely through his fault and through his errors in exercising command and control that the village fell, which resulted in a large number of casualties. A team was put together to investigate these events. I believe Mr. Dzemal Najetovic was the chief investigator, the person who led the investigation team. He later sent a proposal for our commander to be removed. He was eventually removed, but it was after that that I heard that he was actually promoted and was awarded an even higher military rank. This, for me, was highly controversial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you know whether any investigations were conducted into these civilian deaths in Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any investigations and I don't think I ever said anything about any investigations. This is not something that I am familiar with. If I may just add: I did hear, though, that President Izetbegovic had ordered an investigation. I'm not sure who was supposed to be in charge of the investigation or who had received those orders. All I do know is that not much was done about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you hear from that President Izetbegovic had asked for an investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I can't tell you who I heard this from. This was a piece of information that was bandied about in the media, radio, and television. But I can't really point my finger now and tell you such-and-such a person gave me the information. I may have known at the time, it's just that I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all right, Witness. Thank you very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: This will be my examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. The re-examination -- the cross-examination, please, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thanks, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Morrissey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness G.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the photograph Exhibit P298. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I have to address you as Witness G at all times here, and if I slip, everyone must correct me. But the photograph you're being shown here appears to be a photograph of the Uzdol area generally taken from above the school. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is the area generally speaking known as Uzdol and each little small village has its own name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Each hamlet has its own name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the name of the hamlet where the school is to be found is Cer, is that correct, or Cer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm going to ask you to do now is to place certain marks on this map. And what I'll ask you to do is indicate so far as that -- not map, photograph. So far as that photograph shows it, could you put a small circle at places where there were, to your knowledge, fortified HVO positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I can say that there was an accumulation of HVO forces in this area surrounding the school building. Furthermore, I can say that the fortified positions of the HVO were over here and over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Stop there. Thank you. Now, next to -- pardon me. I don't want to cut you off. Are there other fortified positions you can draw with little circles, or is that all that is shown in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: There is more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you draw with the little blue circles those other positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: There is a group of houses that you can see here. This is the hamlet of Bobari. Right above this there was another fortified position, but it's difficult for me to say now where exactly it was. It may have been 200 and 300 metres further to the left or to the right. It was well concealed. In the hamlet itself I believe there was soldiers in the houses. They -- not all of them slept in the school building. I believe some members of the Uzdol battalion - this was the name of the unit - slept in houses in private homes whenever they were off duty. And it's difficult to say now. It's difficult to point at specific houses where some of the soldiers were sleeping.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. Of those three little blue circles that you've marked, is the left-hand one on a hill named Borak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mind just writing the word "Borak" next to that little blue circle.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And would you mind writing the word "Kriz" in the area where the village of Kriz is to be found. Now, I understand that some of it's hidden behind the hill in this photograph, but would you just write "Kriz" in the general area where that village is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Would you please mark in the village of Zelenike.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village of Rajici.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the school, could you just write in the word "Cer."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, using the small blue circles again, such as you did with Borak, would you mind marking in where the tank was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you mark also where the mortar was positioned at the school approximately.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In that photograph, are there any other artillery positions of the HVO shown?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to answer this question. I have no idea what you mean when you say "artillery," what's meant to be included. A 60-millimetre mortar, for example, would not be included under this definition according to the old Yugoslav standards, but it is used to launch shells all the same. These were placed in several different locations, and such weapons would normally be positioned in the vicinity of the front line. That's why it's difficult for me to define artillery with any precision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, well, I understand your answer. And is it also the case that mortars are light artillery and can be moved around quite easily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nevertheless, were there fixed mortar positions which are depicted in that photograph to your recollection or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes. There were fixed mortar positions. I believe these mortar positions were permanent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, in light of that, just to complete this picture, could you put a T next to the circle where the little tank was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And could you draw little blue circles where the fixed mortar positions were to the best of your recollection and mark next to those little blue circles an M for mortar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you indicate when you've completed that task.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I believe I've completed the part that has to do with fixed mortar positions in this particular area; however, the photograph does not show everything. Just to the left of what you can see here there were other artillery positions with pieces trained on the village of Here. And there was a multiple rocket launcher in the area that was used very often. There was also a tank and some other types of artillery weapons, which I can't specify or enumerate for you. There was more artillery to the left than in the village of Uzdol itself. The village to the left that I showed you a while ago, Kranjcici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just so that the Tribunal understands, could you draw a little blue arrow on the left-hand side of the picture and right underneath that little blue arrow the words "other artillery," that arrow pointing to where they are off the picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, would you just indicate on that picture where the village of Here is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I offer that document for tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I guess there's no objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So it's admitted into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's Exhibit D340.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then just leaving that on the screen for a moment, I just have some questions to ask you concerning the -- the military situation of the HVO forces at that time. In the village of Uzdol or the area of Uzdol at that time, approximately how many HVO soldiers did you think there were, based on the information that you had at the time, good or bad?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Our information at the time indicated that there was a battalion that was stationed at Uzdol, an army battalion. However, we had an open view of the road that the HVO units were using. It was easy for us to see any reinforcements that were on their way, soldiers coming and going. We would regularly inform our command about these things. Reports would come from these units that were monitoring the situation in that area, but it was difficult to say anything for sure because the situation kept changing very quickly. As for the general situation, I can tell you that the HVO was far superior to us in terms of equipment and materiel. Sometimes they fired a hundred shells on us in a single day, and we hardly had two to put together. I'm talking about artillery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any tanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No, no tanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What artillery pieces did you have and how much ammunition did you have for those?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: There is something I must clarify, how the situation with artillery developed. At the command of the Independent Prozor Battalion, there was the artillery commander. At first, he didn't have a single piece. Later - and I hope I can remember the exact date - it was the 22nd of January, 1993, we obtained our first 82-millimetre mortar, which was positioned right here on top of this hill. More often than not we had no missiles to use, no shells, or very few if any at all. Later there was several operations where we captured other mortars. Those were 82- and 60-millimetre mortars. I believe it was in the summer of 1993 that two Howitzers came from somewhere around Igman, two 105-millimetre Howitzers, but we had no shells to use. It was once that we managed to obtain three shells, but we used them up in the space of a single day. We only had two Howitzers and only three shells to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And was any extra artillery brought in for the combat operation that took place on the 14th of September, in that sector?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No, no extra artillery. I'm not even aware of being given any shells. If you look at the sort of weaponry that the BH army in the area was in possession of, and specifically I'm talking about 82-millimetre shells, I must say those shells were quite unreliable because the powder charge was normally handmade because we did not have the appropriate material to use for making those. Some of those that we had had been made before the war in those factories over there. They were extremely unreliable, and it was very difficult to determine the degree of accuracy that these shells might have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation. Now, I just want to turn now to the situation of the Independent Prozor Battalion itself, having dealt with the HVO forces there. Into this operation, and I mean the attack on Uzdol on the 14th of September, did the Prozor Independent Battalion commit about 120 to 130 troops on that day, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sorry, just excuse me one moment, Witness G.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I offered that document for tender before but I asked that it be kept on the screen, and now I think it can still be marked, so I think it's best that we tender it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you can still mark on those pictures. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, yes, we're turning to the Independent Prozor Battalion and its situation. Now, you indicated that that battalion consisted mainly of people from the three villages but that some outsiders came to join, and in particular the 25 or so that survived from one of the human chains. And what I wanted to ask you is this: Were you personally able to draw a distinction between HVO extremists on the one hand and innocent local Croatian neighbours of yours on the other hand? Perhaps that was a clumsy question; I'll put it another way. Did you personally want to take revenge on or kill local Croatian civilians of a elderly age or young children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Certainly not. I can even prove that. I'll just name one example. At the time two Croatian villages were BH army controlled, or perhaps I should say two hamlets. One village was at the line of demarcation in no-man's-land. There was a village called Ivanci. And throughout the war there were 13 or 14 civilians living there, among them a young girl aged 9 or 10. The rest of them were mainly elderly persons. If the objective had been to kill civilians, there would have been no need getting our own soldiers killed just to kill a handful of civilians. This could have been done at any time, but it never occurred to anyone to go and do anything like that; that was certainly not our objective. It became a little dangerous at one point in time because many soldiers had suffered some sort of trauma or had a personal thirst for revenge motivated by one thing or another. There was a checkpoint that we had to secure in -- right in the middle of that village, and there was one particular incident that I will now tell you about. The HVO on one occasion shelled the village of Scipe. A teacher was killed outside the school building and a 2-year-old child as well as another young girl who was watching the cattle. Her mother barged into the school. There was a prison inside the school with an HVO captive there. She stormed into the building and attacked this man. At that point, we could no longer afford to keep him there because of the heated atmosphere. We had to move him. Maybe there were even two HVO captives, I can't be sure about it now, who were eventually moved to another prison near Hadzici. I do know, however, that they were eventually exchanged, and they are alive and well. Subsequently we had to set up a checkpoint to protect those Croatian civilians around the clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the history of the Independent Prozor Battalion did not include any history of attacks of a revenge nature or otherwise on civilians. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I believe that that is correct. The Prozor Battalion never wanted to take revenge by attacking the civilian population, nor was it ever issued such a task. And that was the case on this occasion, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And to your understanding, the struggle of the Bosnian army was a struggle to preserve a multi-ethnic Bosnia in which more than just one ethnic group could live. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object to that. I don't think the witness can speak on behalf of the entire Bosnian army. Perhaps he should be asked what he himself felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe your question could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: (redacted)I accept the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness G, I'll just ask the question another way. Was your motivation -- sorry, was it your understanding, your own understanding that the Bosnian army was fighting to defend a multi-ethnic Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I'll try to answer this question in the simplest possible way. The Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, around the beginning of 1993 or towards the end of 1992, I don't know when that document was issued exactly but it's called the Platform of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Wartime. In that document, which we wholeheartedly accepted, the wartime objectives of the ABiH had been expressed. You can see the document for yourself; it's a well-known document. It was adopted by the seven-member Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina which was composed of individuals from all the constituent peoples. As to the legitimacy of the Presidency at the time, that's another issue. But what is important is what is contained in the document. And I am certain that this document states that Bosnia and Herzegovina is a multi-ethnic community, a civil democracy. And that was finally my task. As assistant commander for information, it was my task to inform our troops of the contents of that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: On countless occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you were explaining that document and its meaning to the troops, what were the point -- what were the main points you tried to make to the troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, first of all the troops often asked me whether we had any military objectives, and my only answer was that our military objective was in fact expressed in that platform. And -- in fact, there was nothing else I could refer to when providing official explanations because the position of a certain official institution is far more important than my personal position, the position on the sort of state that we were fighting for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so in explaining it to the troops I take it it was fundamental to that platform that atrocities against other ethnic groups - and in particular atrocities against civilians - were to be avoided at all costs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't mean to cause any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps could we go into the private session for this small moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So anyway, as a result of those matters which we raised in the private session, we don't have to mention again, what you can say is: It was made perfectly clear on numerous occasions that the men of the Independent Prozor Battalion that they shouldn't commit atrocities against civilians of other ethnic groups. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I wish to move on to the question -- some questions arising out of Commander Buza. And perhaps that will take us to the close of these proceedings for this passage as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you excuse me just one moment, please, Witness G, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a bit of a touchy question whether we would finish in the time allowed this afternoon. I'm not sure about it. I would have said no, but it's possible. Given the way the answers came in the end, it's possible. I'm in the Tribunal's hands here. For myself I think it's worth a try, but I can't promise to finish this afternoon. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we arranged the extra sitting for this afternoon just because tomorrow we are not sitting and we hope we could do as much as possible for today. I have no means to -- it does not mean that we should limit your right of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour. I'll press on. Thank you for that indication. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness G, just logistics matters. Now we move to Commander Buza. It's a fact that -- I don't mean to go into the details greatly here. But it's a fact when Commander Buza first arrived he brought in some quite good organisational changes to the Prozor Battalion. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But one of the troubles about Commander Buza was that he after a while began to act as if he was a law unto himself. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it appeared to you at least that he took decisions without consulting his subordinates who might well have known a lot more than he did. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in part, a reason that he advanced for doing that was that he wanted to preserve the security of the information known to the command. Is that one of the reasons that he gave for that not consulting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did Commander Buza -- well, first I should ask you a more general question. Did Commander Buza ever give you a reason why it was he was not consulting with subordinates who had good local knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I believe that he was trying to conceal his reasons. He didn't inform us often. But on the other hand, we could guess what his reasons were on the basis of his behaviour. I'll provide you with an example. For example, when in the area of Prozor municipality we had -- well, in that area we had a house in which the civilian authorities were located and municipal bodies were in that house. And he as the commander told a sabotage unit, Go and open fire around the municipal building a bit to scare them. That was unacceptable for me. And there were various other acts that I could not understand. On one occasion there was an incident that concerned the use of medical supplies. We had a serious problem because we didn't have a GP, a general practitioner, but we did have someone who worked in the field of pharmacy. But the assistant commander for the medical corps was a medical orderly, and he had all the medical supplies in a number of jars. They had all been mixed up, so when this pharmacist came he couldn't understand how it was possible for this system to function. He listened to this pharmacist for a few days and then drove him away and made this medical orderly responsible for those duties again. And there were other absurd situations, other absurd acts. In particular, he used up a lot of fuel, walked around for no particular reason, and we couldn't understand why he would just leave the unit without their commander. And these were the reasons for which we didn't get on with each other. And we had a deputy commander who was well educated and his proposals weren't even listened to. In my opinion, they were simply rejected out of hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. There's just -- we've just reached the end of the session, and there's just one question that I have for you before we stop and that was: Did he have a nickname or a title that he gave himself at that time that he liked to be called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Well, yes. He told us that his nickname was Cigra. Now, I don't really know what Cigra means. It's a sort of attractive toy. In our language it would mean something small and agile, something that should be a source of joy. That's how he would present himself. He presented himself as an experienced soldier who had fought in Algeria and who had been a colonel in the Alger army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That might be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 3.30 in this courtroom. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry for the delay, but anyway we'll sit here until 5.00. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness G. Now, before the break we were speaking of Commander Buza and we asked some general questions about him. Now I have some specific questions about his relations to you. You've already explained some of the problems, but what I want to ask you is: Did he consult you about plans for combat activities in your area after he became commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: He didn't consult me on the whole because I wasn't responsible for planning combat activities. I didn't have such duties, but I know that his Deputy Chief of Staff did play such a role and he did relay information to me. He said that he acted in a very stubborn manner and did not take into consideration arguments that were presented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, who was the chief of military security of the SVB in the Independent Prozor Battalion, and I mean in September of 1993? We've been provided by another witness with the name of Bektas. Do you remember an individual named Bektas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I don't think he was the assistant commander for security. I think Zijo Camatic [phoen] was, but I'm not sure about that because this would change. But I think he was the assistant commander for security and Bektas was involved in the security field, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able now, after 11 years, to recall Bektas's precise role?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I think that for a certain period of time he was the assistant, but that was before. When Mr. Camatic arrived, he took over that position since Buza had appointed him to that post. Naturally, there were certain problems there, too, because, in my opinion, such an appointment should have been made after consultation with other members of the command and having obtained the authorisation from the superior command, and I'm not sure that he asked them for their approval. And afterwards, Mr. Bektas was some sort of official in that security sector, or he was a lower-level official, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to your understanding, if a crime was committed in the area of responsibility of the Independent Prozor Battalion, the professional body with the competence to investigate that was the military security service. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey, please be very cautious and careful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was very obtuse. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope that paper in front of you will help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But anyway, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you for the help. As I say, I made it clear, with my past history, I welcome early intervention rather than late punishment. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that, Witness G. So just to continue, anyway -- well, I want to ask some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could we just go into the private session please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier I was asking you about Commander Buza and the question of whether he was prepared to share information very much. There's a document I want to show you now, and you may or may not have seen this document, so I'm going to ask you to take a quick look at it and tell me if you have. This document is D140; it's an exhibit that's already been tendered. What's going to be shown to you now is a document that is a military proposal that was submitted -- a plan that was submitted to the 6th Corps command, in particular submitted to Salko Gusic, the commander of the 6th Corps, and it was offered by a support staff person called Zukanovic. Now, I'm going to ask you a couple of questions about it. First of all, did you ever see this document yourself? And then after that, I will ask you some questions about the plans that it contains and so on. Do you have that document in front of you on the screen as yet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I can see the first part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Could I ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Or could I just ask the witness be given a chance to read through it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to question you closely on the contents of the document, so there isn't the need to read it tremendously closely, but of course if you want to, you can stop us and ask to have time to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the first page and to see the introductory information, and then shown the last page to show that it's signed off by Mr. Zukanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have the English version of the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just so the court staff know what's happening, once the witness has had a chance to see the last page and inspect the signature, then I want to go back to the start again and ask some questions about that and go back to the first page. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask some formal questions first of all about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Might we go back to the first page now, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, do you know who Mr. Zukanovic is from your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I can see that this is a document from the 44th Brigade, from Jablanica. It was a fairly large mountain brigade and there are many men whom I could not have known in that brigade. And Enes Zukanovic is not really someone I can remember either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I can't remember who he was and what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's okay. Have you ever seen -- I mean, to the best of your memory, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Okay. Well, look, I understand that. I just want to ask you a couple of questions, though. The questions of you don't require you to analyse the document, but I need to while I'm asking you the questions. So do you recall around the time of the 29th of August of 1993 -- let's say the end of August 1993, whether or not there was any discussions between Salko Gusic, the commander of the 6th Corps, and Enver Buza, who was the Independent Prozor Battalion commander at the time, concerning proposed lines of attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: There was contact between them on a daily basis. Our commander was in touch with the corps commander daily. What specifically was said about this is not something that I can tell you. The truth is: I simply don't know. I know that there was much discussion going on on how to coordinate the 44th Jablanica Brigade and the 45th Brigade, which was adjacent to the area covered by our independent battalion. There were several views on how to go about this problem, how to make our situation easier and make things more difficult for the HVO. I know that there were ideas to the effect that we should try and cut some of the roads, to cut the road between the logistics base and the HVO command in Prozor, as well as the road leading south to Jablanica. These views were expressed and debated. I'm not familiar with any details, however. I am aware of a handful of details; I'm not sure if they're relevant. For example, a bridge was mined on one occasion as part of this operation. It was behind the lines, and this was a complex operation which occurred in the summer of 1993. I can't remember whether in July or in August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That may possibly be a little bit earlier for our period, Witness G, but we'll see -- we'll see how we go in relation to that question. Now, was -- was Commander Buza required to brief you on his discussions that he had with Salko Gusic of the 6th Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Generally speaking, we asked the commander many times to keep us up-to-date on what the situation was. Some members of the command were in constant disagreement with him on that count. At one point in time, we got fed up to have to point out the same sort of problem over and over again. I know that there were corps meetings. I know that he went to those meetings. We didn't know what he said at those meetings. All I know is that at one point we received orders to hand over our anti-tank missiles, the Maljutkas, to the corps. It was only later that we learned that this was a result of him boasting at the meeting about having a number of those. But we found out from people from the 2nd Corps who were not involved in our area. There was a small point of contact, but that was all. When things came to a head, he could not comply with that request, obviously. He had to go to the Voljevac commander and ask to be supplied some, but the Voljevac commander was in no position to oblige. All in all, there was a request that came in for us to hand over something that we did not actually have, and this just goes to prove that there was little, if any, communication between the commander on the one hand and us on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to ask you perhaps a more general question as well at that point there. Your unit was the Independent Prozor Battalion. On your left-hand side was located the 44th Jablanica Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: No. On our left-hand side was the 45th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Pardon me. Yes, that's my mistake. I apologise for that. The 45th Brigade on your left, and on your right-hand side, was that where the 317th Brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And on the other side of the 317th Brigade there was a borderline of the 6th Corps, and on the other side of that was a unit attached to the 4th Corps -- sorry, to the 3rd Corps, namely Operations Group West. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Our battalion's area of responsibility, or rather, its far right end, was adjacent to the 6th Corps. And from there on, it was the area of responsibility of the 317th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Now, it's the fact, isn't it, that with regard to the city of Prozor and its liberation there were a number of units that were potentially relevant to that action. Some of them came from the 6th Corps and some of them were part of the 3rd Corps command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that in -- for any -- for any military actions to succeed in respect to the liberation of Prozor, there was an obvious need for some coordination between the 3rd Corps and the 6th Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to ask you a question about an inspection team. Did it come to your knowledge late in August or early in September of 1993 that there was an inspection team headed by Sefer Halilovic and also including some other senior army officers named Karic, Suljevic, and Bilajac in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I don't know what role that team was supposed to play. I'm not sure if it was an inspection team or a command team. I'm not familiar with its specific nature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I met some of those people out in the field. For example, Mr. Suljic, General Halilovic, but I had no authority to ask them about their own powers, nor had anyone told me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was really what my next question was going to be. That is: Did you have authority or was it your place to inquire into the precise role of those senior officers who came to Herzegovina; Halilovic, Karic, Suljevic, and Bilajac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: If circumstances had been normal, the battalion commander would have familiarised me with their role, purpose, and mission, including the role of General Halilovic. However, I can guarantee that he said no such thing, except at one point in time after that first meeting he said that General Halilovic was around and that he would be in charge of the action, or lead the action, if you like. Those were his precise words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recall whether he used the term "rukovodjenje" in that context or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I don't think that word was used. I think the word to lead was actually used. I didn't hear the expression you have just referred to. Maybe I have just forgotten it. Perhaps my recollection is not very specific. Maybe I just can't recall them using the term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's okay. I'm certainly not going to put words in your mouth. But you used the word "vodi"; is that correct? Is that the word that you remember? Or perhaps I should ask you another question. Do you have a memory of the specific word that was used at all, now in 2005?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I distinguish the term "rukovoditi" from the term "voditi," which is not at all the same thing in military terms. However, for truth's sake, I can't commit myself either way right now. I can't say for sure that someone used the term "rukovoditi" in relation to General Halilovic, but they certainly did use the word "voditi" in relation to General Halilovic and the impending action. That's what our commander told us, whatever that meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he go on to explain what that meant? And when I say "he," did Buza, Commander Buza, go on to explain what that meant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: He never bothered to elaborate. He liked to leave things unsaid or maybe not entirely clear. There were some material matters that we were never entirely and properly informed about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Were you ever shown -- or in September of 1993, were you ever shown an order dated 30th of August of 1993 and written by Commander Delic, appointing the inspection team and assigning it particular functions and tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS G
utterances.text: I was never shown this order. I have no idea what it's about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit D146.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Chana.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: In respect of this order, the witness said he has never seen it and what purpose is to be served in showing him this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we need an explanation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
